newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Fears Nobel East Timor peace award could backfire.
newsitem.headline: Fears Nobel East Timor peace award could backfire.

text.p: The Nobel Peace Prize award to two East Timorese could make a settlement more difficult in the troubled territory absorbed by Indonesia 20 years ago, political and diplomatic analysts said on Sunday.
"It's going to make life difficult, and the immediate danger is that it could trigger something down there," one diplomat said.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee on Friday awarded the 1996 peace prize jointly to East Timor's outspoken Bishop Carlos Belo and self-exiled independence activist Jose Ramos-Horta, who now lives in Australia.
The Indonesian authorities regard Belo as an acceptable recipient, but have bitterly attacked the award to Ramos-Horta, described by Foreign Minister Ali Alatas as a "political adventurer".
Analysts said that at best the awards would persuade the Indonesian government that East Timor was not a problem which was going to disappear, and a solution would ultimately have to be found.

"I hope that this will attract more seriousness from the government of Indonesia, and Portugal and the international community to bring a political solution... to the issue, one that can be accepted by all the parties," Florentino Sarmento, who runs a rural development organisation in East Timor, told Reuters from the capital Dili.
But analysts said the award to Ramos-Horta in particular was likely to strengthen demands for independence on the one side, and harden Jakarta's reaction on the other.
"One doesn't feel instinctively that it's going to push peace forward. It may in the short to medium term make things a bit messy," one source said.
President Suharto has firmly rejected suggestions for autonomous rule for the territory.

Sources in the former Portuguese colony, occupied by Indonesia in 1975 and absorbed the following year, said the territory was quiet. However, security has been tightened, ahead of a visit by Suharto to inaugurate several public projects this Tuesday.

Diplomatic and political analysts said the award to Ramos-Horta, who fled the territory three days before Indonesian troops invaded on December 7, 1975, would give him a "global soapbox" from which to preach independence.
But they said there was no question of Indonesia relinquishing sovereignty over the territory, which lies some 2,000 km (1,200 miles) east of Jakarta and 500 km (300 miles) north of Australia.
Diplomatic sources said Australia, New Zealand, the United States and Canada had afforded de facto recognition of Indonesia's claims to the territory through visits by their ambassadors in Jakarta.
"This does not mean they condone the initial action and they still want a political settlement," one source said.

Indonesia has also come under fire for its human rights record and instances of military brutality in East Timor, a territory about the size of Northern Ireland with a mainly-Christian population of around 800,000.
The United Nations has refused to recognise Indonesia's sovereignty and regards Portugal as the administering power. Ambassadors of European Union members still avoid the territory.

The awards were welcomed with varying degrees of enthusiasm by Western nations. But diplomatic sources said Indonesia could expect support from Asian states, particularly its Southeast Asian neighbours, who would regard the Norwegian committee's stated political motives with considerable scepticism.
